title: Ephemeral proxy surge benchmark: TLS resumption and multiplexing notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad for experiments measuring the latency/CPU impact of ephemeral edge proxies that accept short-lived client connections at surge QPS. I want to understand how TLS session resumption and HTTP/2 multiplexing trade off per-request latency vs CPU overhead under realistic small-payload LLM inference calls (prompt ~40 tokens, response ~80 tokens).

Hypotheses: 
- Enabling TLS session resumption (0-RTT or session tickets) will reduce median and tail for cold client connections but increases CPU at the proxy during ticket encryption/decryption.
- HTTP/2 multiplexing on a long-lived upstream connection reduces total TLS handshakes to origin and reduces tail, but can exacerbate head-of-line issues when one request stalls the model-serving pipeline.
- Many ephemeral proxies spun up during a surge (short-lived containers) will make session resumption less effective unless tickets are shared via a K/V store.

Environment / notes:
- Client generator: cheetah-load v0.9 (custom harness) running from 8 client workers across 4 k3s nodes (m5.large-ish equivalent).
- Proxy: rouge-proxy v1.2 (in our staging image) configured as ephemeral sidecar; two modes tested: "bridge-mode" (one TLS termination per client) and "mux-mode" (HTTP/2 client-facing, pooled HTTP/2 upstream to origin).
- Origin model endpoint: local Raptor runtime (g4dn.xlarge-ish) with small LLM stub returning synthetic token stream (to control jitter).
- Payload: POST /v1/generate, JSON bodies 1.2KB; responses 3.4KB. Aim: small-ish requests to emphasize handshake/RTT costs.
- Test patterns: 1) Sudden 1500 QPS spike from 0 -> steady for 120s; 2) microbursts: 10s bursts reaching 2500 QPS repeated every 30s; 3) baseline steady 200 QPS.

Key config knobs tried:
- TLS: session_tickets enabled/disabled; session_timeout 300s vs 30s; 0-RTT enabled/disabled (for clients that support it).
- Keepalive: client keepalive idle 30s vs 5s; upstream keepalive 120s.
- HTTP/2: multiplexing on/off; max concurrent streams upstream 100 vs 16.
- Proxy pool churn: ephemeral TTLs 45s vs 300s (how long a proxy instance stays alive after last request).

Commands / approximate scripts (for reproducibility):
- spawn clients: cheetah-load --rps 1500 --duration 120 --pattern spike --concurrency 8 --client-id X
- collect metrics: promql queries for proxy_tls_handshakes_total, proxy_cpu_seconds_total, request_latency_seconds{quantile="0.99"}, http2_streams_opened_total

Aggregate results (representative runs):
1) Bridge-mode (no mux), TLS tickets disabled, ephemeral TTL 45s
- median latency: 92 ms
- p95: 310 ms
- p99: 980 ms
- proxy CPU (avg across fleet): 56% during spike (8 cores total across nodes), TLS handshakes/sec: ~1200
- observations: many requests observed extra 1 RTT compared to steady baseline; p99 dominated by TLS handshake queuing on proxy under CPU pressure.

2) Bridge-mode, TLS tickets enabled (session_timeout 300s), ephemeral TTL 45s
- median: 70 ms
- p95: 180 ms
- p99: 420 ms
- proxy CPU: 62% (slightly higher), TLS handshakes/sec: 380 (resumed sessions) + 350 full per-second during initial spike
- observations: large improvement in tail, but CPU went up due to ticket crypto (AES-GCM operations). Ticket sharing between ephemeral proxies not configured, so benefit mostly for clients that reconnected to the same proxy instance.

3) Mux-mode (client HTTP/2, upstream pooled HTTP/2), TLS tickets enabled, upstream max_streams=100, ephemeral TTL 45s
- median: 65 ms
- p95: 150 ms
- p99: 240 ms
- proxy CPU: 71% (more multiplex bookkeeping + stream state), http2 active streams peaked at 220 across pool
- observations: tail improved vs bridge-mode with tickets because fewer full TLS handshakes to origin and client-facing multiplexing amortizes per-connection cost. However, saw intermittent bursts where a stalled stream to origin (model warmup) delayed other streams sharing same upstream connection -> manifested as micro tail spikes ~500ms.

4) Mux-mode but upstream max_streams=16 (more conservative)
- median: 72 ms
- p95: 210 ms
- p99: 380 ms
- proxy CPU: 63%
- observations: reducing max_streams reduced head-of-line risk and CPU slightly but increased p95/p99 because more upstream connections were opened (more TLS). This is a clear trade-off point.

5) Mux-mode + shared ticket store (Redis-backed ticket key sync across proxies), TTL 45s
- median: 60 ms
- p95: 140 ms
- p99: 210 ms
- proxy CPU: 68%
- notes: sharing tickets reduced redundant full-handshakes across ephemeral instances. Best p99 so far while keeping CPU moderate. Redis latency added negligible overhead (multi-get on start of new proxy instance).

Microburst pattern (10s bursts to 2500 QPS) highlights:
- Bridge-mode without tickets: proxy CPU saturates and time-to-first-byte jumps; p99 > 2s in worst runs.
- Mux-mode with shared tickets: much better resilience; p99 often < 300ms but occasional 800ms spikes tied to origin model queueing (not proxy).

Quick ASCII sketch (p99 over time for a representative burst):
Time(s): 0    10   20   30   40  50 60
NoTickets:  1200 1800 1700 900 400 200 120
WithTickets:  420 460 380 220 150 110 90
WithTickets+Mux+Redis: 210 240 200 160 130 100 80

Conclusions / quick takeaways: 
- For ephemeral proxy fleets that spin frequently during surge, TLS session tickets are very high ROI if tickets are made shareable across instances (Redis/consul). Without sharing, benefits are limited to client affinity scenarios.
- HTTP/2 multiplexing gives the best steady p50/p95 but introduces head-of-line sensitivity; mitigate by conservative max_streams and request-level timeouts to abort stalled streams early.
- CPU tradeoffs: enabling ticket crypto raises CPU but reduces TLS handshakes overall; multiplex bookkeeping also costs CPU. For our fleet, ticket sharing + mux yields the best p99 per CPU used.
- Microbursts are more about origin queueing and model pipeline variance than proxy handshakes once tickets+pooling are enabled. Need to add origin-side admission control and request tail trimming.

Open questions / TODOs: 
- Test 0-RTT semantics safely (replay concerns) for our payloads; check whether small prompt payloads are safe to accept with 0-RTT.
- Repeat runs with real model stack (not stub) to capture model pipeline stalls interacting with multiplexing.
- Explore TLS offload hardware (nginx+ssl-engine) vs software crypto for ticket ops.
- Quantify cost: compute per-1M requests CPU-seconds and translate to $ at reserved capacity.

Notes to self: save raw Prometheus dumps (run id: ephem-20241102-leyla-01). Archive cheetah-load scripts and exact rouge-proxy config into gitlab MR referenced above.

End of scratchpad.
